name: Budapest School
summary: The Budapest School was the circle of Georg Lukács's students and colleagues (Ágnes Heller, Ferenc Fehér, György Márkus, Mihály Vajda) that moved from Marxist humanism to radical democracy. Its members revived the early Marx's theory of radical needs, condemned Soviet-type societies as totalitarian dictatorships over needs, and held that socialism is inconceivable without democracy and pluralism. Heller and Márkus later accepted markets, representative democracy with liberal rights and the welfare state, while seeking workplace co-management and a radicalised democracy.
scope: Lukács's students, especially Heller, Fehér and Márkus (with Vajda, and Kis and Bence on Márkus's economic critique), from the 1960s to their later work: democratic socialism, the critique of Soviet-type societies (Dictatorship over Needs, 1983), the theory of radical needs (Heller 1976), Heller's 1982 socialist-objective lecture and her 1999 Theory of Modernity. It excludes Lukács's own orthodox period and the later dissident liberals. Heller's late interviews on Orbán count at low confidence, since only she states them. Full texts of Dictatorship over Needs, Eastern Left, Western Left and Márkus's books were not available; their arguments are taken from Heller's own essays and the scholarship, so many themes are silent.

sources.usedFor: Accessible abstract documents socialism as long-term democratic experiment rather than a single Soviet blueprint.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Heller's 1982 text says outright that the Soviet system is neither socialist nor capitalist, and Beilharz reports that Fehér and Heller held the state-capitalist label too lazy an analysis for Soviet-type societies, which they treated as a distinct type.

worker-ownership.rationale: Heller proposes long-term state loans so workers who want to can buy a factory and run it as a collective enterprise, alongside co-management of nationalised industry; she gives no general programme of worker ownership.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Heller's 1982 essay calls co-management (self-government) in factory, office and store the first and fundamental condition of radical democracy, since democracy otherwise stops at the factory gate, and says nationalisation would not change that.

socialized-markets.rationale: Márkus, Kis and Bence concluded that no socialist economy can do without a market and that an association of free producers is incompatible with abolishing it (a regulated market economy); Heller sees no reason a market with co-managed firms must fail.

central-planning.rationale: Márkus, Kis and Bence held that no socialist economy can do without a market and that the labour-value axiom behind central planning is a fiction; the trio describe the Soviet bureaucracy as inefficient by design, and Heller finds state-run production no remedy.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Márkus, Kis and Bence's critique of Marx's Capital rests on rejecting the labour theory of value as an abstract fiction; only this strand states it and the rest of the school is not recorded on the point.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Strands differ: the early radical-needs writings keep the associated-producer ideal, while Márkus, Kis and Bence hold that no socialist economy can do without money and the market.

public-ownership.rationale: Heller says nationalising certain large industries might even prove unavoidable, but denies that nationalisation brings democratic socialism and finds a general nationalisation programme bleak; she takes no firm side.

cut-welfare.rationale: Heller criticises the welfare state as bureaucratic, centralist and paternalist, and wants it de-paternalised step by step, but says monetarist cuts cannot cure its ills and that its institutions securing a minimum of security should be kept.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Heller's theory of radical needs treats rebellion against the manipulation of needs in consumer societies as vital, her 1982 essay calls the ideology of saturated needs and superabundance false, and in 1999 she rejects equating the satisfaction of all needs with progress.

alienated-labor.rationale: Heller's early theory of need holds that capitalist production alienates people from their needs and frustrates their talents through the division of labour, and her 1982 essay wants co-management to reunite manual and intellectual work and end the monotony of modern labour.

independent-unions.rationale: Heller's 1982 essay faults the British TUC for refusing to stand by Solidarity until Polish workers had dissolved the state unions, and says workers' parties must back the dominated against those who rule.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Heller says the three logics of modernity are related but none determines the others, and Beilharz notes Fehér and Heller held that base and superstructure would never do.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Heller rejects a single fixed theory of history in favour of contingency, and Fehér and Heller separated political from socioeconomic classes, so class conflict is not their main driver of history.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Fehér and Heller made the state and bureaucracy an independent centre of power in their Weberian turn, so that after Polanyi it cannot be treated as derivative of capital.

one-party-rule.rationale: The trio call every East European society totalitarian however tolerant, insist socialism cannot be conceived without democracy, and say pluralism is outlawed there; Heller's 1982 essay sides with the oppositions against the rulers.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: The trio hold socialism inconceivable without democracy and condemn Soviet-type rule as dictatorship, and Heller says radical democracy needs majority support and strict parliamentary rules.

vanguard-party.rationale: Heller rejects party functionaries who claim to embody universality, holds that emancipation is always self-emancipation, and Grumley reports Heller and Fehér's axiomatic opposition to politics in which one party speaks for others.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Heller's 1982 essay urges workers' parties to support the East European opposition movements against the rulers, and ends on Luxemburg's line that socialism is free pluralism in every sphere of life.

party-controls-media.rationale: Heller's 1982 essay lists breaking the monolithic character of the mass media among the measures radical democracy needs, and the trio fault Soviet-type societies for outlawing pluralism.

total-state.rationale: The trio call Soviet-type societies totalitarian, Grumley reports Fehér and Heller defined the dictatorship over needs by the total character of its politics, and Heller treats the totalitarian party-state as the modern invention to be resisted.

strong-leader.rationale: Heller calls Orbán a Bonapartist and his elected power concentration a tyranny, and in her theory of modernity the division of powers and independent courts belong to legitimate rule.

workers-councils.rationale: Heller praises the 1956 demand for dual power, councils together with freely elected parliaments and several parties, and says she was never against representation, so councils are not offered in place of parliament.

direct-votes.rationale: Heller calls pure direct democracy terroristic and keeps representation and rights as safeguards, while the school still affirms direct participation alongside them.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Heller's 1982 essay defines socialism as a radicalisation of democracy in which the whole population discusses social problems and takes part in decisions at every level, beginning with co-management of workplaces.

decide-locally.rationale: Heller says the more active the population, the less centralist decisions should be, and calls for decentralisation and de-paternalisation of the welfare state step by step.

state-harmful.rationale: Heller's essay assigns the state loans, funding and legal safeguards, and her theory of modernity says the modern state draws legitimacy from protecting citizens against violence.

separated-powers.rationale: Heller's theory of modernity describes the division of powers and independence of the judiciary as part of legitimation by law, and names liberal democracy the best institution for modernity.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Heller says pure democracy without safeguards is pure terror and that liberalism protects the minority from the tyranny of the majority, so institutions must constrain majorities.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Heller defends human rights as the counterweight to unchecked majority rule and lists the liberal rights (property, coalition, conscience, speech, privacy, fair trial) that protect persons from the political.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Heller says democracy can be reduced to a formal shell of periodic elections, and in 2018 she called Orbán's elected regime a tyranny, saying modern democracy is liberal democracy.

elective-rulers.rationale: In Heller's account modern democracy combines majority rule with elected representatives, so that people obey only laws they made themselves, which leaves no place for a hereditary throne.

natural-rulers.rationale: Heller grounds modern social relations in symmetric reciprocity: all are born free and equally endowed with reason and conscience, and the modern world is not a pyramid.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Heller states that all men and women are born free and equally endowed with reason and conscience, and that modern relations are symmetric, not a hierarchy of birth.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Heller says she was never against representation and defended the 1956 demand for freely elected parliaments and several parties.

person-over-state.rationale: Heller's theory of modernity makes the single person the building block of modern society and has liberalism shield the person from the tyranny of the political; Grumley notes the authors' opposition to others speaking for persons.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Heller states that all are born free and equal in reason and conscience, treats equality before the law as the core liberal right, and Grumley reports freedom and equality as the universal value ideals of her theory.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Heller distinguishes individual, citizen and minority or group rights, and says some group rights, such as aboriginal land claims, are justified by past injustice.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Heller says that when marks of race or gender become significant in political identification, politics turns into biopolitics and falls short of granting liberal rights and political liberties.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Heller and Fehér note that biopolitics entered world politics on the side of racism, and Heller makes equality before the law the central liberal right.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Heller says religion and art disclose Truth and give life Meaning, calls Marx's view of religion shaped by a narrow-minded rationalism, and builds her ethics on existential choice rather than reason alone.

religion-illusion.rationale: Heller calls Marx's view of religion as an opiate narrow-minded, though she grants that knowledge now accumulates in science, not religion; she credits religion with disclosing truth and meaning.

abortion-legal.rationale: Grumley reports that Heller and Fehér's sympathies in the abortion debate are clearly pro-choice: the woman is the custodian of the potential life and the one who must choose.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Heller says modernity's values place limits on treating all cultures as equally worthy, so a culture rejecting human rights may rightly have that claim rejected, though she adds it still cannot be treated as unworthy.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Heller places the Bolshevik and Nazi states in one modern type, the totalitarian state, naming Auschwitz and the Gulag together, while noting they differ, since Bolshevism totalised society and Mussolini's Italy did not.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Heller speaks of the exterminating camps of totalitarian states and of Auschwitz as a historical event, and counts the Holocaust among her own formative experiences.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Heller called ethnic nationalism a negative ideology and a kind of nihilism that rulers use as a tool of power; this is her late statement, with no matching one from the others.

nation-first.rationale: Heller's 1982 essay says preferring pragmatism to principle in international affairs, out of short-sighted national egoism, is always bad, and that workers' parties should back democracy worldwide.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Grumley reports that Márkus and Heller both held the European Union to be a bearer of progressive politics that must be championed against populism and totalitarianism, though it should be radically democratised.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Fehér and Heller's Doomsday or Deterrence defends deterrence, rejects unilateral disarmament and calls the anti-nuclear movement's choice of life over freedom a failure of courage.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Fehér and Heller called the demand to withdraw American missiles from Europe a naive capitulation to Soviet manipulation.

revolution-justified.rationale: Heller calls the 1956 Hungarian rising the only really socialist revolution in history and backs the East European liberation movements, though she distrusts a total revolution and favours radical democracy.

direct-action.rationale: Heller's 1982 essay says radical democracy has no chance without majority support and the strict keeping of parliamentary rules, placing change in elections and public debate.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Heller's 1982 essay builds socialism on parliamentary democracy and existing state institutions in the West, but endorses dismantling the tyrannical apparatus of Soviet-type states: the answer depends on the state confronted.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Grumley reports Fehér and Heller held the Enlightenment's promise of mastering nature disappointed, with science able to liberate but also to destroy, and Heller rejects science as a source of absolute truth.

notes:
Members diverged: Márkus kept more of a Marxist economic critique (market within a socialist economy, labour theory of value rejected) and opposed US military adventurism, while Heller supported the US invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq and was more optimistic about progress, per Grumley (s7). Statements on markets and the labour theory therefore rest on Márkus's strand and are low confidence. Themes searched without a stated position: ecology, immigration, religion in public life, gender, criminal justice, foreign policy outside the Cold War, monetary and tax policy. Full texts of Dictatorship over Needs, Eastern Left, Western Left, Beyond Justice and the Márkus books are borrow-only or unavailable, so Fehér's and Vajda's own positions are thinly covered. Source texts used: Heller 1982 (Spanish), A Theory of Modernity, Grumley, Beilharz.

claude-sonnet-5-5+GPT-6.1-Sol notes: Independent re-audit using old sources only as leads. Full primary interview and joint essay were downloaded; the scanned essay was OCR-read, with its layout checked on a rendered page. The Theory of Need excerpt and scholarly study supplied the needs and economic themes. The thin world theme was researched through the authors’ own discussion of Soviet intervention and national independence; later Fehér–Heller nuclear-deterrence work was located but not imposed on the school’s earlier common scope. Searches of government, culture, society, liberty, means, ecology and technology found no basis for generic policy answers on religion, ethnicity, drugs, energy or digital technology. General anti-nationalism does not become six unrelated firm answers. Later Heller positions on welfare, indigenous claims or abortion are not automatically a shared Budapest School platform.
